sec.title: Aims
sec.p: No studies have comprehensively compared the efficacy of sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, renin–angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor neprilysin (ARN) inhibitors based on different type of heart failure, including heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). The aim of this network meta‐analysis was to evaluate the relative efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitor (SGLT2i), RAS inhibitor (RASi) and ARN inhibitor (ARNI) in different types of heart failure.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A systemic literature search was performed from inception to 19 November 2022 for randomized control trials assessing the risk of cardiovascular (CV) death or hospitalization for heart failure (HHF) of these drugs in HF. A network meta‐analysis was performed. Risk ratio (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were synthesized.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Seventeen studies were selected with a total of 61 489 patients. In patients with HFrEF, ARNI led to a reduced risk of a composite outcome of CV death or HHF when compared with placebo (RR = 0.83, 95% CI 0.77–0.89). Similar trends were observed when focusing on the outcome of CV death or HHF alone. In patients with HFpEF, SGLT2i showed the beneficial effects on the CV death or HHF events when compared with placebo and RASi (RR = 0.82, 95% CI 0.74–0.92; RR = 1.16, 95% CI 1.02–1.31). For CV death, all these three drugs could not show beneficial effects in HFpEF. For the incidence of HHF in HFpEF, both SGLT2i and ARNI demonstrated the beneficial effects but SGLT2i was superior to ARNI. There were no differences in the events of discontinuation under these drugs when compared with placebo or each other in either HFrEF or HFpEF patients. SGLT2i showed the least renal injury among these interventions in HFrEF and there were no differences in the incidence of renal injury of these interventions in HFpEF.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Among these drugs, ARNI showed the greatest ability to lower the incidence of CV death or HHF and SGLT2i exerted the least renal injury in patients with HFrEF. In patients with HFpEF, SGLT2i was associated with a reduction in the risk of CV death or HHF. There were no differences in the incidence of renal injury of these interventions in HFpEF. The intolerance of these drugs were comparable in both HFrEF and HFpEF.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The prevalence of heart failure (HF) is dramatically increased worldwide. The incidence of HF is closely associated with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and obesity. HF is composed of patients categorized by their symptoms and ejection fraction (EF), including those HF with reduced EF (LVEF ≤40%; HFrEF), midrange EF (EF between 40% and 49%), and preserved EF (EF ≥ 50%; HFpEF). 1 Improve health status of these patients is becoming a key goal of HF management. To date, the impacts of several pharmacotherapies on HF have been evaluated.

Renin–angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors, including angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers, have been shown to reduce the risk of mortality in patients with HFrEF. 2 , 3 In addition, sacubitril‐valsartan, the first‐in‐class angiotensin receptor neprilysin (ARN) inhibitor, improves the ratio of all‐cause mortality in chronic HFrEF patients when compared with the intervention of RAS inhibitors. 4 Sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, originally identified as glucose‐lowering drugs, offer important cardiorenal protections in HFrEF regardless of the diabetic status. 5 , 6 On the contrary, classic RAS inhibitors treatment could not convincingly reduce mortality in HFpEF. 7 , 8 , 9 Compared with RAS inhibitors, ARN inhibitors did not show beneficial effects in reducing total hospitalization for HF (HHF) and cardiovascular (CV) death in the status of HFpEF. 10 Recently, the improvement of mortality by SGLT2 inhibitors during the treatment of HFpEF has been identified when compared with placebo. 11

However, data directly comparing these drugs are lacking, which limits the choice of clinicians between them. We therefore conducted a network meta‐analysis to evaluate the relative efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitor (SGLT2i), RAS inhibitor (RASi) and ARN inhibitor (ARNI) in different types of HF.

sec.title: Literature research
sec.p: This network meta‐analysis was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items For Systematic Reviews and Meta‐analysis). 12 We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception to 19 November 2022. The following keywords were applied: [‘Sodium‐Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors’ (MeSH) OR ‘SGLT‐2 inhibitor’ OR ‘SGLT‐2’ OR ‘empagliflozin’ OR ‘dapagliflozin’ OR ‘canagliflozin’ OR ‘luseogliflozin’ OR ‘ertugliflozin’] OR [‘angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitor’ (MeSH) OR ‘angiotensin receptor antagonist’ (MeSH) OR ‘RAS inhibitor’ OR ‘renin‐angiotensin system inhibitor’ OR ‘angiotensin receptor blockers’ OR ‘angiotensin receptor‐neprilysin inhibitor’ OR ‘ACE inhibitor’ OR ‘ARN inhibitor’ OR ‘ACEI’ OR ‘ARNI’ OR ‘ARB’ OR ‘captopril’ OR ‘enalapril’ OR ‘cilazapril’ OR ‘fosinopril’ OR ‘lisinopril’ OR ‘perindopril’ OR ‘ramipril’ OR ‘candesartan’ OR ‘irbesartan’ OR ‘losartan’ OR ‘telmisartan’ OR ‘valsartan’ OR ‘olmesartan’ OR ‘eprosartan’ OR ‘sacubitril‐valsartan’] AND [‘heart failure’ (MeSH)] AND [‘myocardial infarction’ (MeSH) OR ‘coronary artery disease’ (MeSH) OR ‘cardiovascular disease’ (MeSH) OR ‘stroke’ (MeSH) OR ‘mortality’ (MeSH) OR ‘cerebrovascular disorders’ OR ‘MI’ OR ‘CVA’ OR ‘cerebrovascular accident’ OR ‘MACE’ OR ‘major adverse cardiovascular event’ OR ‘death’ OR ‘cardiovascular mortality’ OR ‘HF hospitalization’ OR ‘heart failure hospitalization’ OR ‘HF hospitalization’ OR ‘hospitalization for HF’ OR ‘HHF’]. We restricted the search to human studies published in the language of English.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: Studies were selected based on the following criteria: (i) They were designed as random controlled trials (RCTs) comparing SGLT2i or RASi or ARNI with placebo or each other; (ii) they included adult patients (age ≥18 years) with specificized kinds of HF; (iii) they provided the incidence of a composite outcome of CV death or HHF.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The efficacy outcome was a composite of HHF and CV death including myocardial infarction and stroke.

sec.title: Data extraction and quality assessment
sec.p: All data from eligible studies were independently extracted by two reviewers. Any disagreements were discussed and evaluated by a third reviewer. For each study, we extracted the following data: baseline participants characteristics, interventions, follow‐up duration, number of participants, and the incidence of CV death and HHF. We also collected the number of events related to discontinuation and renal injury in these studies. The Cochrane risk of bias assessment was applied to assess the quality of each study, including sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, and selective outcome reporting. 13 Risk of bias was judged as unclear, high, or low.

sec.title: Data synthesis and analysis
sec.p: The comparison of different interventions was made using a frequentist approach for each endpoint. 14 Risk ratio (RR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were assessed for the association between the intervention and the incidence of events. Ranking probabilities for all treatments were estimated to obtain a treatment hierarchy using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA). Risk of bias was assessed by Cochrane Collaboration's tool. The overall heterogeneity was evaluated with the I 2 statistic, with values of >25%, >50%, and >75% representing low, moderate, and high levels of heterogeneity, respectively. The pairwise comparison and network analysis were performed using R and Stata software.

sec.title: Literature search and included studies
sec.p:
From 3398 articles initially identified, we selected 17 studies involving a total of 61 489 participants (Figure
1A ). The basic characteristics of the included studies were summarized in Table
1 . The mean age of patients was 66.6, with a median follow‐up time ranging from 0.5 to 4.2 years. Of the 17 included studies, nine studies assessed the effects of SGLT2i or RASi or ARNI in HFrEF, 2 , 3 , 4 , 6 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 and six studies focused on HFpEF. 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 20 Meanwhile, 2 studies included the results from both HFrEF and HFpEF patients. 5 , 21 We identified 6 trials comparing SGLT2i with placebo, 5 , 6 , 11 , 16 , 20 , 21 eight trials comparing RASi with placebo, 2 , 3 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 17 , 18 , 19 and three trials comparing ARNI with RASi. 4 , 10 , 15 At present, there are still no published or ongoing trials directly comparing the CV outcomes of these drugs. According to the Cochrane Collaboration's tool for assessing risk of bias, all trials met the criteria for low risk of bias (Figure S1 ).

sec.title: The composite CV outcome of different treatment in HFrEF and HFpEF
sec.p:
Figure
2 demonstrates the network comparisons of available treatments in patients with HFrEF and HFpEF. The composite CV outcome in patients with HFrEF was available in 10 trials. 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 21 SGLT2i, RASi, and ARNI were associated with a lower risk of CV death or HHF (23%, 15%, and 30%, respectively) as compared with placebo (Figure
3A ). Compared with RASi, ARNI significantly decreased the occurrence of CV death or HHF (RR = 0.83, 95% CI 0.77–0.89). The composite CV effects were no different in the treatment of RASi and ARNI when compared with SGLT2i (Figure
3A ). SUCRA score showed that the treatment of ARNI was ranked first in reducing CV death or HHF, followed by SGLT2i and RASi (Table S1 ). The overall heterogeneity for CV death or HHF was low (I 2 = 0%) in patients with HFrEF (Table
S2 ).

caption.p: Network plot of available interventions in (A) HFrEF and (B) HFpEF. The numbers indicate the number of trails included in the comparison.
Network meta‐analysis of available interventions for the composite outcome of CV death/HHF in (A) HFrEF and (B) HFpEF.

sec.p:
Seven studies reported the composite outcome of CV death or HHF in patients with HFpEF. 5 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 11 , 20 , 21 SGLT2i showed the strongest ability in decreasing the incidence of CV death or HHF (RR = 0.83, 95% CI 0.77–0.90) (Figure
3B ). Compared with placebo, RASi was not associated with the decreased risk of CV death or HHF (RR = 0.95, 95% CI 0.89–1.02). SGLT2i treatment could significantly decrease the composite CV outcome (RR = 1.14, 95% CI 1.04–1.27) when compared with RASi. SUCRA score demonstrated that the treatment of SGLT2i was ranked first in reducing CV death or HHF in HFpEF (Table S1 ). The overall heterogeneity for CV death or HHF was low (I 2 = 0%) in patients with HFpEF (Table
S2 ).

sec.title: The CV death outcome of different treatment in HFrEF and HFpEF
sec.p:
For 11 trials reporting the CV death in patients with HFrEF, 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 21 all the available treatments conferred a benefit (Figure
4A ). ARNI showed the greatest relative reduction in the occurrence of CV death compared with placebo (RR = 0.74, 95% CI 0.64–0.86) (Figure
4A and Table
S1 ). Accordingly, ARNI treatment was associated with a decreased risk for CV death as compared with RASi (RR = 0.82, 95% CI 0.72–0.94) (Figure
4A ). There were no differences in the comparison between ARNI/RASi and SGLT2i (Figure
4A ).

caption.p: Network meta‐analysis of available interventions for the CV death outcome in (A) HFrEF and (B) HFpEF.

sec.p:
Eight trials demonstrated the results of CV death in patients with HFpEF. 5 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 20 , 21 However, none of the three treatments demonstrated the beneficial effects in reducing CV death when compared with placebo or each other (Figure
4B ). The overall heterogeneities for CV death were low (I 2 = 5%; I 2 = 0%) in both patients with HFrEF and HFpEF (Table
S2 ).

sec.title: The HHF outcome of different treatment in HFrEF and HFpEF
sec.p:
There were 10 trials containing the HHF outcomes in patients with HFrEF. 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 All three treatments were associated with a decreased risk of HHF compared with placebo (Figure
5A ). Among them, ARNI demonstrated the strongest beneficial effects (RR = 0.65, 95% CI 0.54–0.79) (Figure
5A and Table
S1 ). There were no differences in reducing the occurrence of HHF when compared with each other (Figure
5A ).

caption.p: Network meta‐analysis of available interventions for the HHF outcome in (A) HFrEF and (B) HFpEF.

sec.p:
For seven trials offering the HHF outcomes in patients with HFpEF, 5 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 11 , 20 , 21 SGLT2i and ARNI treatment could significantly reduce the HHF risk when compared with placebo (24% and 20%, respectively) (Figure
5B ), and SGLT2i treatment was ranked first based on SUCRA score (Table S1 ). Compared with RASi, both SGLT2i and ARNI treatment demonstrated the beneficial effects in decreasing the incidence of HHF (Figure
5B ). SGLT2i showed a greater efficacy (Table S1 ). There was no difference between ARNI and SGLT2i in lowering the HHF risk (RR = 1.05, 95% CI 0.90–1.22). The overall heterogeneities for HHF were low (I 2 = 8%; I 2 = 0%) in both patients with HFrEF and HFpEF (Table
S2 ).
The discontinuation and renal injury of different treatment in HFrEF and HFpEF.

Nine studies reported the number of events related to discontinuation or renal injury in patients with HFrEF. 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 15 , 17 , 18 , 19 There were no differences in the occurrence of discontinuation of the three treatments when compared with placebo or each other (Figure
6A ). Five studies contained the data about discontinuation or renal injury in patients with HFpEF. 7 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 20 There were no differences in the occurrence of discontinuation of the three treatments when compared with placebo or each other (Figure
6B ).

caption.p: Network meta‐analysis of available interventions for discontinuation in (A) HFrEF and (B) HFpEF.
Network meta‐analysis of available interventions for renal injury in (A) HFrEF and (B) HFpEF.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The present network meta‐analysis included the most updated studies, providing the most comprehensive evaluation of SGLT2i, RASi, and ARNI on the CV outcomes in different types of HF. The results indicated that ARNI showed the greatest benefits in reducing the incidence of CV death/HHF in patients with HFrEF. In addition, SGLT2i could significantly improve the risk of CV death/HHF in patients with HFpEF.

According to our data, in the group of patients with HFrEF, all these three drugs could reduce the composite outcome of CV death/HHF. Among them, ARNI shows the highest probability to be superior to SGLT2i and RASi. Similar trends are observed when focusing on the outcome of CV death or HHF alone. Aimo et al.'s network meta‐analysis indicated that SGLT2i was not associated with lower risk of CV death or HHF compared with ARNI based on the comparison between two SGLT2i trials and one ARNI trial in HFrEF. 22 However, our network meta‐analysis contains three SGLT2i trials and two ARNI trials, suggesting ARNI's greater efficacy in reducing the outcomes of CV death or HHF in HFrEF. What is more, the beneficial effects of SGLT2i could be displayed in both diabetic and non‐diabetic patients. However, whether ARNI's efficacy is related with the diabetic status still remains unknown.

In the group of patients with HFpEF, only SGLT2i could decrease the composite outcome of CV death/HHF. For CV death, all these three drugs could not show the beneficial effects. For the incidence of HHF, both SGLT2i and ARNI show the beneficial effects, but SGLT2i are superior to ARNI. The prevalence of HFpEF is gradually increasing; however, there were no approved suitable drugs for this kind of HF. Based on our analysis, SGLT2i intervention could cause a significant decrease in risk of CV death or HHF.

These drugs exert beneficial effects on heart failure via different mechanisms. SGLT2i may protect from heart failure by decreasing blood pressure and arterial stiffness, reducing preload and afterload and increasing haematocrit. 23 The mechanisms underlying the CV benefits of SGLT2i may be related to the simultaneous upregulation of nutrient deprivation signalling and downregulation of nutrient surplus signalling mediated by autophagy, as manifested by an increase in the expression and activity of adenosine monophosphate–activated protein kinase (AMPK), sirtuin 1, sirtuin 3, sirtuin 6, and peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor γ coactivator 1‐α (PGC1‐α) and decreased activation of mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR). 24 RASi reduces sodium and water retention via inhibition of RAS. 25 ARNI is a novel drug combined the RAS blockade with natriuretic peptides (NP) enhancement. ARNI contains valsartan and sacubitril in a 1:1 ratio. Sacubitril is a precursor of metalloprotease inhibitors, which inhibits the cleavage of brain natriuretic peptides and other peptide substrates. 26

Evaluating the relative efficacy of different drugs is important for clinicians choosing optimal treatment. However, there still lack trials directly comparing these drugs. This aim could be addressed by an indirect comparison based on the results of RCTs through a comprehensive approach such as network meta‐analysis. In this analysis, ARNI had a higher SUCRA score than other two drugs for the outcome of CV death/HHF during the status of HFrEF; SGLT2i ranked first in patients with HFpEF. Given the indirect nature of comparison, head‐to‐head comparison between different interventions should be conducted in the future.

Furthermore, we also evaluated the tolerance and safety of these drug in patients. We collected the numbers of discontinuation in patients under different interventions, and there were no differences of the three treatments when compared with placebo or each other in either HFrEF or HFpEF, suggesting the comparable tolerance of these drugs with placebo. The adverse effects of SGLT2i include hypoglycaemia, renal injury, and genital/urinary tract infection, whereas the adverse effects of RASi and ARNI contain hypotension, renal injury, elevation of plasma potassium, and angioedema. We compared the occurrence of renal injury, the common side effects of these drugs, in these patients. In patients with HFrEF, only SGLT2i treatment is associated with a lower risk of renal injury when compared with placebo. When compared with RASi and ARNI, SGLT2i is also less harmful to renal function. In addition, ARNI causes less renal injury events when compared with RASi. However, in patients with HFpEF, the effects on renal injury were comparable between these drugs and placebo.

The present study includes 17 studies published by 19 November 2022, which contains very large numbers of participants and high quality of trials. In contrast, there are several limitations in our network meta‐analysis. Firstly, there were little head‐to‐head trials directly comparing these drugs; therefore, the comparative effects were generated with indirect evidence. Secondly, different drugs were used in each intervention. There could exist with‐class differences. Thirdly, there were differences in trial designs, patients' characteristics, and background therapies. Finally, owing to unavailable patients' data, we avoided to analyse the effects of these drugs in subgroups, such as stratified by age, ethnicity, or the presence of diabetes.

To sum up, ARNI showed the greatest ability to lower the incidence of CV death or HHF and SGLT2i exerted the least renal injury in patients with HFrEF. In patients with HFpEF, SGLT2i was associated with a reduction in the risk of CV death or HHF. There were no differences in the incidence of renal injury of these interventions in HFpEF. The intolerance of these drugs was comparable in both HFrEF and HFpEF. However, given the limitations in this study, real‐world data in the future should confirm the findings from current network meta‐analysis.
